name: Recognising increasing and decreasing patterns
description: Students identify whether a pattern made with numbers, shapes or objects is increasing or decreasing by a constant amount, and name the constant term being added or subtracted.
exampleOfSuccess: Given a pattern like 3, 6, 9, 12 the student says it goes up by 3 each time and correctly identifies the next term as 15.
commonError: Student describes the pattern in general terms (it gets bigger) without identifying the constant amount.
checkpointTask: Show me this pattern: 2, 5, 8, 11. Is it increasing or decreasing? By how much each time?
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M2N04 (add and subtract) as students use addition and subtraction to identify the constant term.

name: Continuing a pattern sequence with materials
description: Students use physical or virtual materials to continue an additive pattern for at least 3 more terms, applying the identified constant term.
exampleOfSuccess: Given 4 counters, 7 counters, 10 counters arranged in groups, the student adds 3 more each time and builds the next two terms correctly.
commonError: Student copies the most recent term rather than applying the rule, creating a repeated element instead of continuing the pattern.
checkpointTask: Here are some blocks in a pattern: 1, 4, 7. Build the next two terms using blocks.

name: Creating a pattern sequence from a given rule
description: Students create their own additive pattern sequence using a teacher-specified constant (e.g. make a pattern that goes up by 4) with numbers, shapes or objects.
exampleOfSuccess: Given the rule increase by 5, the student writes 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and can explain why each term follows the rule.
commonError: Student applies the rule inconsistently, skipping or doubling the constant in some steps.
checkpointTask: Make a pattern that starts at 6 and increases by 3. Write the first 5 terms.

name: Identifying missing elements in a pattern
description: Students locate and fill in missing terms within a pattern sequence, using the constant term to work forwards or backwards.
exampleOfSuccess: Given 5, [?], 15, 20, [?], the student correctly identifies 10 and 25 using the rule add 5.
commonError: Student guesses missing terms without checking against the rule, producing terms that do not fit the pattern.
checkpointTask: Fill in the missing numbers: 3, [?], 9, [?], 15. How did you work them out?

name: Recording patterns and describing the rule
description: Students record an additive pattern as a number sequence, write a description of the rule in their own words, and verify a classmate can replicate it from the description.
exampleOfSuccess: The student writes 2, 7, 12, 17, 22 - add 5 each time and a classmate successfully continues it to 32.
commonError: Student describes the pattern by listing terms rather than stating the rule, so the description cannot be used to generate the sequence.
checkpointTask: Write a pattern of your own. Write down the rule so someone else can continue it without seeing your original.
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M2N04 as students use two-digit addition to generate and verify terms.

name: Recognising additive patterns in the environment
description: Students identify and describe additive patterns observed in real-world contexts such as tiling, stair steps or number charts, connecting the pattern to a constant term.
exampleOfSuccess: Looking at a staircase diagram, the student says each step adds 2 more blocks so it goes 2, 4, 6, 8 and identifies this as an additive pattern increasing by 2.
commonError: Student notices the visual pattern but cannot connect it to a numerical rule or constant term.
checkpointTask: Look at this tiling pattern. Can you see a number pattern? What is the rule?
reviewNotes: nan | AUDIT: Marked optional - from elaborations, not a named CD verb. Useful enrichment but not required for mastery.

name: Building part-part-whole knowledge to 10
description: Students use materials or ten-frames to represent all combinations that make each number to 10, recording the related addition facts.
exampleOfSuccess: Given 7, the student names all pairs: 0+7, 1+6, 2+5, 3+4 and reverses, using a ten-frame without counting.
commonError: Student can only recall some combinations and reverts to counting on fingers for others.
checkpointTask: Using a ten-frame, show me all the ways to make 8. Write each one as a number sentence.

name: Using doubles facts to 20
description: Students recall doubles facts (1+1 through 10+10) fluently and use them as anchors for near-doubles strategies.
exampleOfSuccess: The student instantly recalls 6+6=12 and uses it to solve 6+7 by saying that is one more than 12, so 13.
commonError: Student knows doubles but does not connect them to near-doubles, treating each fact as isolated.
checkpointTask: What is 7+7? Now use that to work out 7+8. Explain your thinking.
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M2A03 as doubling is a foundation for multiplication facts for twos.

name: Bridging to 10 for addition
description: Students use knowledge of combinations to 10 to bridge through 10 when adding, partitioning one addend to complete the ten then adding the remainder.
exampleOfSuccess: To solve 8+5, the student partitions 5 into 2+3, adds 8+2=10, then adds 3 to get 13, without counting.
commonError: Student attempts to count on from the larger number rather than bridging, losing track before reaching the answer.
checkpointTask: Solve 9+6 without counting. Show me how you used 10 to help.

name: Recalling addition facts to 20 fluently
description: Students demonstrate rapid recall of all addition facts with totals to 20 without needing to count or use materials.
exampleOfSuccess: When shown a flashcard for 7+8, the student responds 15 within 3 seconds without visible counting strategy.
commonError: Student recalls facts for small numbers quickly but still counts on for facts involving larger single digits.
checkpointTask: Answer each addition fact as quickly as you can.

name: Deriving related subtraction facts
description: Students use known addition facts to derive and record the related subtraction facts, understanding the inverse relationship.
exampleOfSuccess: Knowing 9+6=15, the student writes 15-6=9 and 15-9=6 and explains subtraction undoes addition.
commonError: Student treats subtraction as a completely separate operation, not connecting it to known addition facts.
checkpointTask: You know that 8+7=15. Write two subtraction facts that use the same three numbers.
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M3A01 (inverse relationship) as a precursor skill.

name: Applying addition facts in two-digit calculations
description: Students extend known facts to solve two-digit additions, using place value partitioning and known single-digit facts.
exampleOfSuccess: To solve 34+5, the student says I know 4+5=9 so 34+5=39 using the known fact directly.
commonError: Student reverts to counting on for two-digit calculations, not recognising the embedded single-digit fact.
checkpointTask: Solve 27+6. What single-digit fact helped you?

name: Systematising addition facts to find patterns
description: Students record addition facts systematically (e.g. all facts for a given sum) to identify and explain patterns.
exampleOfSuccess: The student records all facts that equal 12: 3+9, 4+8, 5+7, 6+6, 7+5, 8+4, 9+3 and notices the pattern of swapping addends.
commonError: Student records facts randomly without noticing patterns, missing some and duplicating others.
checkpointTask: Write all the addition facts that equal 10. What pattern do you notice?
reviewNotes: nan | AUDIT: Marked optional - enrichment beyond CD verbs. CD covers recall, proficiency, extend, apply, develop subtraction facts; all met by IC01-IC06.

name: Connecting doubling language to multiplication
description: Students recognise that double, twice and multiply by 2 all describe the same operation, and demonstrate this with materials.
exampleOfSuccess: Given 4 counters, the student says double 4 is 8, that is the same as 2 groups of 4, that is 2 times 4.
commonError: Student understands double as a concrete action but does not connect it to the multiplication symbol or language.
checkpointTask: Show me double 5 with counters. Write it as a times fact.
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M2N05 (multiply and divide) as doubling is the first multiplication fact set.

name: Building the twos multiplication sequence
description: Students count by twos and use materials or arrays to build and record the multiplication facts for 2 (2x1 through 2x10).
exampleOfSuccess: The student skip-counts 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and links each count to a fact: 2 twos is 4, 3 twos is 6 while touching each pair in an array.
commonError: Student skip-counts correctly but cannot link the count to the corresponding multiplication fact.
checkpointTask: Count by twos to 20. Point to each step and say the matching times fact.

name: Recalling multiplication facts for twos fluently
description: Students demonstrate rapid recall of all multiplication facts for 2 (2x1 through 2x10) without needing to skip-count.
exampleOfSuccess: When asked 6 times 2, the student responds 12 within 3 seconds without audibly counting in twos.
commonError: Student knows the answer but arrives at it by skip-counting from 2 each time, relying on the sequence rather than recall.
checkpointTask: Answer each times-2 fact as quickly as you can. No counting!

name: Deriving division facts using halving
description: Students use knowledge of multiplication facts for 2 to derive the related division facts, connecting halving to dividing by 2.
exampleOfSuccess: Knowing 2x7=14, the student writes 14 divided by 2=7 and explains halving undoes doubling.
commonError: Student treats division by 2 as a separate skill, not connecting it to known multiplication facts.
checkpointTask: You know 2x9=18. Write the two division facts that use the same three numbers.
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M2N05 (multiply and divide) as division facts for 2 link to equal sharing and grouping.

name: Applying doubling and halving in practical contexts
description: Students apply doubling and halving to solve simple practical problems, choosing the operation that fits the situation.
exampleOfSuccess: When told there are 6 students and each needs 2 pencils, the student doubles 6 to get 12 without prompting.
commonError: Student understands doubling abstractly but does not recognise when a problem situation calls for it.
checkpointTask: There are 8 tables in the room. Each table has 2 chairs. How many chairs altogether? How did you decide to double?

name: Extending twos facts beyond 2x10
description: Students apply understanding of the twos pattern to calculate 2x11, 2x12 and beyond, using place value and known facts.
exampleOfSuccess: The student says 2x12 - I know 2x10=20 and 2x2=4 so 2x12=24, using partitioning rather than counting.
commonError: Student can recall facts to 2x10 but treats larger multiples as unknown, reverting to counting.
checkpointTask: What is 2x15? You do not need to count. What do you already know that helps?
reviewNotes: nan | AUDIT: Marked optional - extension content. CD scope is multiplication facts for twos (2x1 through 2x10); beyond is enrichment.

name: Connecting twos facts to odd and even numbers
description: Students use knowledge of multiplication facts for 2 to identify even numbers as multiples of 2 and explain why others are odd.
exampleOfSuccess: The student says 18 is even because 2x9=18, it is in the twos. 17 is not in the twos so it is odd.
commonError: Student can identify even and odd numbers by rote but cannot explain the connection to multiplication by 2.
checkpointTask: Is 16 even or odd? How do your twos facts help you know?
reviewNotes: Cross-descriptor link candidate: connects to AC9M4N02 (properties of odd and even numbers) as a foundational concept. | AUDIT: Archived - odd/even properties is AC9M4N02 (Year 4 content). Cross-descriptor link note retained but not appropriate as a core IC here.
